Buyer's Guide: What Actually Matters

Five things decide whether a tool set fits your home. Ignore the piece-count bragging; check these.

01

Piece count

39 pieces covers the basics; 180–230 covers most homes and cars; 322 is the “never buy another” tier. More pieces is not automatically better — a 39-piece set with the right tools beats a 300-piece set full of bits you’ll never use.

02

Drive sizes

Sockets come in 1/4″, 3/8″ and 1/2″ drives. 1/4″ is for small fasteners, 3/8″ does most home and car work, 1/2″ handles the big bolts. A set with all three (like the DEWALT here) means one case for every size.

03

Ratchet teeth

More teeth means a smaller swing — a 72-tooth ratchet works in tight spots where a coarse ratchet can’t move at all. It’s the one spec that tells you how the tool feels in a cramped engine bay or behind a cabinet.

04

Storage

A hard case travels well, a bag is lighter to carry room to room, and a drawer box is best if the tools live in one place. Buy the storage that matches where the tools will actually live.

05

SAE vs metric

American cars and older hardware use SAE (inches); imports, bikes and most new furniture use metric. A set with both means you never hit a bolt your set can’t turn — the DEWALT here covers both, and most full-size sets do the same.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many pieces do I actually need?

For a first home, 39 pieces covers hanging, assembling and basic fixes. If you also work on a car or do regular DIY, 180–230 pieces is the comfortable middle — enough sizes without the bulk. Past 300 pieces you’re mostly buying bits and duplicates, useful only if the household does a lot of different jobs.

What’s the difference between 1/4″, 3/8″ and 1/2″ drive?

It’s the size of the square hole that connects a socket to a ratchet. 1/4″ is for small fasteners and tight spaces, 3/8″ is the all-rounder for most home and car work, and 1/2″ is for large bolts and high torque. Sets with all three drives, like the DEWALT on this page, cover everything with one case.

Do I need both SAE and metric?

Probably, yes. American cars and older hardware use SAE (inches), while imports, bicycles and most new furniture use metric. A set missing one system will eventually meet a bolt it can’t turn. Full-size mechanics sets almost always include both — check the listing before you buy.

Is a bigger set always better?

No. Piece count includes every bit, adapter and accessory, so a 322-piece kit and a 180-piece kit may have a similar number of actual tools. What matters is whether the set has the sizes and tools your jobs need — and storage you’ll actually use.

Hard case, bag, or drawer box — which storage is best?

It depends where the tools live. A hard case is best for carrying to the car or a job. A bag is lighter for carrying room to room. A drawer box, like the CRAFTSMAN here, is best when the tools stay in one place — everything visible at once, and it goes back together in seconds.

Are these sets good gifts?

Yes — a tool set is one of the most useful gifts for a new homeowner or graduate. The Apollo 39-piece set is the easy gift: small, affordable and useful on day one. The DEWALT 192-piece set is the big gift for someone setting up a whole home or garage.

The Bottom Line

For most new homeowners, this decision is simple: the DEWALT 192-Piece Set does the most jobs in one case, and it’s the set we’d buy first. Spend less with the Crescent if budget matters, pick the CRAFTSMAN if you want your tools stored in drawers, take the WORKPRO if you want the most pieces for home repairs, and give the Apollo to anyone starting from zero.
